title: Jason and Medea: The Flight
subtitle: A brother's death, a pursued ship, and a homecoming with a cost

main.author: Apollonius Rhodius
main.locator: Argonautica 4, Jason kills Apsyrtus; Book 4, normalized characters 25208-25981
main.excerpt: And Jason went to the ambush to lie in wait for Apsyrtus and then for his comrades. But he, beguiled by these dire promises, swiftly crossed the swell of the sea in his ship, and in dark night set foot on the sacred island; and faring all alone to meet her he made trial in speech of his sister, as a tender child tries a wintry torrent which not even strong men can pass through, to see if she would devise some guile against the strangers. And so they two agreed together on everything; and straightway Aeson’s son leapt forth from the thick ambush, lifting his bare sword in his hand; and quickly the maiden turned her eyes aside and covered them with her veil that she might not see the blood of her brother when he was smitten. And Jason marked him and struck him down

narrativeBlocks.title: Pursuit across the sea
narrativeBlocks.body: Aeetes launches his fleet after the fleeing Argo. The fastest way to slow a pursuing king is the one act in this story no one can take back — Medea's brother Apsyrtus is killed, in some tellings lured into an ambush by her own message.

narrativeBlocks.title: A guilt that needs cleansing
narrativeBlocks.body: The murder of kin — especially a brother betrayed by a sister — is one of the deepest pollutions in Greek thought. The fugitives must seek ritual purification at Circe's island (the same Circe Odysseus meets) before they can go on.

narrativeBlocks.title: The long way home
narrativeBlocks.body: The return voyage scatters them across half the known world — sirens, clashing shores, the bronze giant Talos on Crete. The Argo reaches Greece at last, but every mile home has been paid for.

narrativeBlocks.title: Iolcus, and no throne
narrativeBlocks.body: Jason presents the fleece — and Pelias, predictably, does not hand over the kingdom. Medea's revenge is the signature act of their partnership: she persuades Pelias's daughters that chopping their father to pieces will restore his youth. Pelias dies by his daughters' hands.

narrativeBlocks.title: The pattern deepens
narrativeBlocks.body: Quest stories usually end at the homecoming. This one keeps going: each 'victory' leaves a debt — Apsyrtus, Pelias, the abandoned father in Colchis — and the debts all land on Jason and Medea together.
